eMudhra revokes 8 more CA certificates after private key mishap

eMudhra revoked eight additional intermediate CA certificates after finding its key-transfer script exposed RSA private-key material in host memory, bringing the incident total to 16 affected intermediates. The company is exiting the publicly trusted TLS certificate business after browsers and operating-system vendors blocked the compromised certificate chains.
KEY POINTS
  • 01eMudhra revoked eight additional RSA intermediate certificate authority certificates on November 7 after determining that its transfer process handled private-key information in host computer memory rather than solely within protected hardware.
  • 02The additional revocations bring the total to 16 affected intermediate certificates, including eight ECDSA certificates whose private keys were reduced to one byte by a bug in a custom Python script.
  • 03The same Python script was used in April 2025 to move certificate authority keys between hardware security modules from different vendors after delays obtaining new hardware.
  • 04Mozilla, Google, Apple, and Microsoft released protections to block trust in the compromised eMudhra certificate chains.
  • 05eMudhra plans to leave the publicly trusted TLS certificate business and stop issuing certificates under its remaining G1 hierarchy by November 16.

eMudhra revoked eight additional RSA intermediate certificate authority certificates after its investigation found that private-key information was handled in the memory of the computer running a custom transfer script. The revocations bring the total to 16 affected intermediates, including eight ECDSA certificates whose private keys were reduced to a single byte by a bug in the script. eMudhra said it could not show that the RSA keys were handled according to its certificate security policy, even though they were not weakened in the same manner as the ECDSA keys.

The script was created to move certificate authority keys between hardware security modules from different vendors after delays obtaining new hardware, and it was used in April 2025. The investigation also found that a June 2025 issue involving revocation lists signed by nonmatching keys was an early warning sign, but its cause was not investigated at the time. Mozilla, Google, Apple, and Microsoft released protections to block trust in affected certificate chains, and eMudhra said it will exit the publicly trusted TLS certificate business and stop issuing under its remaining G1 hierarchy by November 16.

  • A June 2025 mismatch between certificate revocation lists and their corresponding certificate authority keys was an early warning of the flawed key-generation process, but eMudhra corrected the signing mismatch without investigating its cause.
  • The eight additional RSA intermediate certificates were revoked because eMudhra could not show that their private keys had been handled in accordance with its own security policy, even though those keys were not weakened in the same way as the ECDSA keys.
  • Some of the affected RSA intermediates had actively issued TLS and code-signing certificates from May 2026 through November 3, so eMudhra replaced or migrated affected customer certificates.
  • The investigation found that eMudhra did not check generated private-key strength or confirm that keys used to sign certificates matched the keys originally generated within its protected hardware.
  • Despite the severity of the key-handling failures, eMudhra stated that it has not found evidence that the compromised keys were used maliciously.

eMudhra, a company that issues digital certificates used to prove websites and software are genuine, canceled eight more certificates after finding flaws in how it handled secret security keys. Earlier flaws made eight other keys so weak that they could be guessed almost immediately, while the newly canceled certificates may have exposed key information on a regular computer instead of keeping it in protected hardware. The problem could have let criminals create convincing fake website certificates and intercept supposedly private communications, affecting people and organizations that relied on those certificates. Major browser, operating-system, and software companies have blocked the affected certificates, and eMudhra plans to stop issuing publicly trusted website certificates.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a high-impact certificate authority incident affecting 16 intermediate certificates, including keys that could be recovered with minimal effort and RSA keys that were handled outside protected hardware. Major browser and operating-system vendors blocked the affected trust chains, making the event broadly relevant to organizations relying on TLS and code-signing certificates.

Baker Tilly Advisory Group is notifying certain clients that an unauthorized actor obtained data stored on a platform operated by an unnamed third-party service provider. The firm became aware of the potential incident on September 6, 2026, and completed its review of the affected data on October 28, 2026. Baker Tilly said it contained the incident, engaged external experts, and notified law enforcement.

The company has not disclosed the total number of affected people, the provider involved, or the precise information exposed in its sample notice. However, the Texas Attorney General reports that 10,456 people in Texas were affected and lists Social Security numbers, full names, addresses, and other information among the exposed data types. Baker Tilly says someone obtained personal information belonging to some of its clients and their dependents from a system run by an outside service provider. The exposed information may include names, home addresses, Social Security numbers, and other details; more than 10,000 people in Texas were affected. This matters because such information can be used for identity theft or fraud, although Baker Tilly says it has not received reports tying either to this incident and is offering affected people two years of monitoring services.

eBPF Rootkits: Why Underground Actors Are Taking Notice

Sponsored research warns that eBPF rootkit techniques are increasingly circulating on underground forums, enabling Linux implants to hide processes, inspect or alter traffic, and evade traditional kernel-module checks. Defenders should inventory eBPF programs, restrict BPF privileges, monitor suspicious attachment points and XDP activity, and patch BPF-related flaws promptly.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Flare reported finding Russian-language underground forum posts that shared eBPF rootkit source code and step-by-step instructions for hiding processes and triggering implants with crafted network packets.
  • 02Unlike traditional Linux rootkits that load kernel modules, eBPF-based malware can use the kernel-supported bpf() interface, so routine lsmod checks may not detect it.
  • 03The article cites BPFDoor, Symbiote, ebpfkit, TripleCross, Boopkit, and LinkPro as examples of malware or research demonstrating BPF or eBPF-based stealth and packet-triggered capabilities.
  • 04Synacktiv reported in October 2025 that LinkPro used eBPF programs to hide host activity and activated its backdoor after receiving a specially crafted packet.
  • 05The article recommends that Linux operators audit loaded eBPF programs with bpftool, restrict unprivileged BPF access and relevant capabilities, monitor for suspicious network triggers and XDP programs, and promptly patch BPF verifier flaws.

Flare reported that underground forums and Pastebin posts are circulating eBPF rootkit code, tutorials, and related exploit material. A Russian-language forum tutorial reportedly included source code for hiding processes, encrypting command-and-control traffic, and activating an implant with a TCP SYN packet using a specific window size. The article presents this as a shift from conference research and isolated threat activity toward wider underground sharing of eBPF-based techniques.

Unlike conventional Linux rootkits that use loadable kernel modules, eBPF programs operate through the kernel-supported bpf() interface and may not appear in routine lsmod checks. The article cites BPFDoor, Symbiote, ebpfkit, TripleCross, Boopkit, and LinkPro as examples of BPF or eBPF-enabled stealth, traffic inspection, concealment, or packet-triggered activation. It recommends auditing loaded programs with bpftool, limiting BPF-related privileges, watching for unexpected XDP programs and suspicious network triggers, and promptly patching BPF verifier flaws.

  • eBPF programs can pass the kernel’s built-in safety verifier yet still be malicious, because the verifier treats approved malicious programs like other valid eBPF programs.
  • LinkPro reportedly attempted to hide its eBPF programs from bpftool prog list, but investigators could still identify associated BPF maps and links, showing the value of comparing multiple host data sources.
  • A purported kTLS and eBPF sockmap privilege-escalation proof of concept claimed support for all Linux kernels from version 4.18 onward, but the article notes that upstream Linux 4.18 lacks a required BPF helper and that success on Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04 was not verified.
  • The underground tutorial described using XDP to inspect unencrypted incoming web traffic and discard packets from 43 IP addresses associated by its author with antivirus vendors.

The article says that code and instructions for hiding malicious software inside Linux computers are now being shared on underground forums. These tools can hide running programs, watch or alter network traffic, and wait for specially made internet messages before activating, making them harder to spot with common checks. Organizations that run Linux servers, including businesses that rely on them for online services, could be affected if attackers gain access, so they need to keep systems updated and check for unfamiliar programs running deep inside the system.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This sponsored trend piece highlights underground sharing of eBPF rootkit techniques and references known examples such as LinkPro, but it does not report a new active campaign, breach, or urgent vulnerability. It is useful background for Linux defenders, yet primarily provides evergreen detection and hardening guidance.

CISA flags Cisco BroadWorks flaw as actively exploited in attacks

CISA added Cisco BroadWorks flaw CVE-2026-20320 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after attackers began exploiting the unauthenticated XXE bug to read sensitive files and steal credentials. Organizations using BroadWorks should urgently apply Cisco’s patches, particularly where OCI-P services are exposed.
KEY POINTS
  • 01CISA added Cisco BroadWorks vulnerability CVE-2026-20320 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog after confirming it is being exploited in attacks.
  • 02CVE-2026-20320 is an unauthenticated XML external entity flaw in the BroadWorks Open Client Interface XML parser that can allow remote attackers to read sensitive configuration information through crafted XML messages.
  • 03Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies were ordered to secure affected systems by November 24 under Binding Operational Directive 26-04.
  • 04Malbear Labs reported that a Chinese-speaking threat actor used a jailbroken DeepSeek Flash model to exploit the flaw against a European telecommunications provider and 13 organizations using its data centers and cloud infrastructure.
  • 05According to Malbear Labs, the reported intrusion recovered a system identity private key, three SSL credential sets, and three additional private keys from the targeted BroadWorks XSP host.

CISA has added CVE-2026-20320, a high-severity Cisco BroadWorks vulnerability, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog after confirming it is being abused in attacks. The flaw affects the Open Client Interface XML parser and can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to read sensitive configuration information by sending a crafted XML message to the OCI-P service. Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies must secure affected systems by November 24 under Binding Operational Directive 26-04. CISA also urged private-sector organizations to prioritize remediation because exploitation is ongoing.

Cisco BroadWorks is a cloud communications platform used by telecom carriers and managed service providers to provide business phone, voice, and collaboration services. Malbear Labs reported that a Chinese-speaking threat actor used a jailbroken DeepSeek Flash model to exploit the flaw against a European telecommunications provider and 13 organizations using its data centers and cloud infrastructure. According to Malbear Labs, the attackers obtained a system identity private key, three SSL credential sets, and three other private keys from the targeted BroadWorks XSP host. Possession of the system identity key could allow impersonation of the XSP in communications between BroadWorks components.

  • The reported targeting of one European telecommunications provider extended to 13 organizations using its data centers and cloud infrastructure, illustrating that compromise of a service provider can affect downstream customers.
  • The stolen BroadWorks system identity key could allow an attacker to impersonate the XSP when communicating with other BroadWorks components, rather than merely exposing configuration data.
  • Malbear Labs found that the BroadWorks Provisioning Server was exposed through an unauthenticated directory listing, creating an additional exposure alongside the XML parsing flaw.
  • CISA’s two-week federal remediation deadline applies only to federal civilian agencies, but the agency explicitly urged private-sector organizations to prioritize the flaw because attacks are ongoing.

The U.S. cybersecurity agency CISA says criminals are actively using a flaw in Cisco BroadWorks, software that phone companies and service providers use to deliver business calling and collaboration services. The flaw can let an outsider send a specially made message and read sensitive information from affected systems without needing to sign in. One reported campaign targeting a European telecom provider reportedly stole digital keys and login-related certificates, which could let attackers pretend to be part of the provider’s own system. CISA has told U.S. federal agencies to fix the issue quickly and urges all organizations using the software to do the same.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a must-read alert on active exploitation of an unauthenticated Cisco BroadWorks flaw that can expose sensitive files and credentials. CISA has added it to the KEV Catalog and set a short remediation deadline for U.S. federal agencies, while reported attacks affected a telecom provider and downstream organizations.

Active ScreenConnect attacks breach MSPs, impact dozens of organizations

Attackers are compromising MSP ScreenConnect environments to deploy rogue remote-access clients across customer endpoints, with at least six MSPs and 286 devices affected so far. MSPs should review Run Command and account activity, revoke sessions, reset credentials from trusted devices, enforce MFA, and avoid interactive sessions with suspected compromised endpoints.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Huntress identified an active campaign in which attackers compromised cloud-hosted ConnectWise ScreenConnect environments used by managed service providers to deploy rogue ScreenConnect clients to customer devices.
  • 02As of Huntress's report, the campaign had affected six managed service providers, at least 286 endpoints, and 47 organizations, with victim counts still increasing.
  • 03The attackers use ScreenConnect's Run Command feature to install remote-access clients that connect outside the legitimate managed service provider's ScreenConnect environment.
  • 04ConnectWise advised partners to avoid interactive ScreenConnect sessions with suspected compromised devices, review account activity, revoke active sessions, reset credentials from a trusted device, and verify multifactor authentication.
  • 05Huntress said its telemetry currently points to compromised credentials and hijacked managed service provider support sessions, although the initial access method has not been determined.

Huntress reported an active campaign targeting managed service providers that use cloud-hosted ConnectWise ScreenConnect. Attackers are compromising these environments and using ScreenConnect’s Run Command feature to install rogue ScreenConnect clients on customer devices. Huntress had identified six compromised MSPs, more than 286 affected endpoints, and 47 organizations, with those figures continuing to rise.

The rogue clients provide attackers with remote access outside the legitimate MSP’s ScreenConnect environment. Huntress also warned that a technician’s workstation could potentially be compromised when the technician opens a ScreenConnect session with an infected customer device, though the mechanics of this reported reverse-pivot technique are unclear. ConnectWise said it is investigating and advised partners to avoid interactive sessions with suspected compromised devices, review account activity, revoke active sessions, reset credentials from a trusted device, and verify multifactor authentication.

Huntress has not determined how the attackers initially gained access, but said its telemetry points to compromised credentials and hijacked MSP support sessions. Sequential attacker-assigned tags suggest other MSPs may have been compromised earlier, prompting ScreenConnect users to check their Run Command histories even if they received no alerts. A malicious batch script uploaded to VirusTotal in July 2026 used one of the rogue client identifiers and attempted to add Microsoft Defender exclusions, establish persistence, download installers, and notify attackers through Telegram, although its relationship to the current MSP campaign remains unclear.

  • The reported risk extends beyond customer endpoints: Huntress warned that a technician’s own workstation could be compromised when the technician opens a ScreenConnect session to an infected customer device.
  • Sequential attacker-assigned tags indicate that additional managed service providers may have been compromised before this campaign was publicly identified, so organizations should check Run Command history even without an alert.
  • One rogue ScreenConnect client identifier appeared in a malicious batch script uploaded to VirusTotal in July 2026, showing that the identifier was associated with earlier malicious activity, although its connection to the current MSP campaign remains unconfirmed.
  • The earlier batch script attempted to weaken Microsoft Defender protections, establish startup persistence, install remote-access software, and notify attackers through Telegram after confirming installation.

Attackers have broken into some companies that provide IT support to other businesses and are using ConnectWise ScreenConnect, a tool that lets technicians control computers remotely, to install their own remote-control software on customer devices. Huntress has identified six affected IT service providers and more than 286 devices at 47 organizations, and says the number may rise. This matters because the attackers could gain control of many businesses’ computers through a trusted support service, and could potentially target the support workers’ own computers when they connect to an infected customer device.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This reports an active, expanding compromise campaign against cloud-hosted ConnectWise ScreenConnect environments, affecting MSPs and dozens of customer organizations. It includes concrete indicators and urgent defensive guidance, while the potential compromise of technician workstations raises the impact beyond individual endpoints.

Maersk confirms data breach as WhiteArmor ransomware demands $5 million

Maersk confirmed a breach of an isolated legacy system tied to its former LF Logistics business, while WhiteArmor claims it stole about 100GB of data and demands $5 million. Maersk says there is no evidence of sensitive-data disclosure or disruption to its broader operations.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Maersk confirmed that a threat actor breached a local system associated with a company it previously acquired, while its investigation remains ongoing.
  • 02WhiteArmor ransomware listed Maersk on its leak site and demanded $5 million in Bitcoin, claiming to have stolen about 100GB of data from the OCF/LF Logistics platform.

Maersk confirmed that a threat actor breached systems belonging to a company it previously acquired, with the incident reportedly isolated to a local system. The company says its investigation is ongoing and that current evidence shows no sensitive data has been disclosed. Maersk also says it does not expect operational disruption and that customers can continue booking and managing shipments normally.

WhiteArmor ransomware claimed responsibility and demanded $5 million in Bitcoin, alleging it stole roughly 100GB of data from Maersk’s OCF/LF Logistics platform. The group claims the data includes nearly 30,000 driver records, plaintext passwords, 33 SUPER_ADMIN accounts, signed delivery receipts, inventory records, and mobile-device logs containing phone numbers, emails, and IMEI numbers. Maersk says it has found no indication that other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems connected through APIs and EDI were affected, and it will provide updates if impacted parties need to be notified.

  • WhiteArmor’s claimed data includes plaintext passwords and 33 highly privileged SUPER_ADMIN accounts, making the alleged theft more consequential than a collection of contact details alone.
  • Maersk says systems used by customers and partners through API and EDI connections show no indication of impact, despite the alleged compromise of the local system.
  • Maersk specifically warned recipients to verify unexpected messages about the incident through their usual company contact, reflecting the possibility of misleading communications tied to the event.

Shipping company Maersk says someone broke into a local older system connected to LF Logistics, a company it bought in 2022, and took data. A group calling itself WhiteArmor is demanding $5 million and says it has information such as driver records, delivery receipts, passwords, and mobile-device details. Maersk says it has found no sign that sensitive information was released or that customers’ shipment bookings and deliveries are disrupted, but people whose information may be involved could still be affected if the claims are confirmed.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a confirmed breach involving Maersk, a major global shipping and logistics company, alongside a named ransomware group demanding $5 million. Microsoft says its November 2026 cumulative updates resolve USB audio problems caused by Windows security updates released since September. The issue affected USB Audio Class 1.0 devices on some Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server 2012 or later systems. Users reported no sound output, unresponsive volume and sound settings, and Device Manager messages stating that the device could not start with Code 10.

Microsoft had previously issued out-of-band updates on September 14 for devices using 8-channel or 3D audio modes, but the November 10, 2026 security update KB5132061 and later updates address the remaining symptoms. Microsoft recommends installing the latest security update because it includes this fix along with other improvements and issue resolutions. For users unable to install the update immediately, some have reportedly restored audio by switching affected devices to 2-channel mode, though Microsoft has not provided an official workaround.

  • The audio failure was not limited to consumer PCs: it also affected Windows Server 2012 and later, making it relevant to both client and server environments.
  • Microsoft’s September 14 out-of-band updates addressed only the 8-channel and 3D-audio symptoms, while the November security updates resolved the remaining USB audio issues.
  • Although Microsoft has not published an official workaround for systems that cannot install the November updates, some users reported that switching to 2-channel audio restored sound.
  • The same November 2026 cumulative updates also resolved Outlook sign-in and mail-delivery problems on Exchange Server systems caused by October Windows Server security updates.

Microsoft says its November 2026 Windows updates fix a problem that could stop some USB-connected speakers and other sound devices from working after earlier security updates. The issue affected some Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server users, causing missing sound, unusable volume controls, or errors saying the device could not start. Installing the latest security update is important because it restores affected audio while also including other fixes and improvements.

Organizations should urgently patch Qlik Sense, ActiveMQ, and Veeam systems and investigate suspicious scheduler.exe, OpenSSH, and scheduled-task activity.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Cynet detected unsuccessful PowerShell reverse-shell attempts against several European Union-based Qlik Sense environments during a period of just over three minutes in October 2026.
  • 02The PowerShell command was executed under scheduler.exe and attempted to connect to 45.115.26[.]23 on port 4455 using a one-line reverse shell.
  • 03The observed activity overlaps with a November 2023 campaign linked to the CACTUS ransomware operation that exploited Qlik Sense flaws for initial access.
  • 04Cynet found that the operator's exposed infrastructure included a Windows Go backdoor, OpenSSH persistence scripts, an Apache ActiveMQ exploit for CVE-2023-46604, and a modified Veeam toolchain for CVE-2024-40711.
  • 05A second PowerShell-script variant attempted to install OpenSSH and create a scheduled task named WinUpdCheck that ran a reverse shell every five minutes.

Cynet detected unsuccessful attempts to deliver PowerShell reverse shells to several European Union-based Qlik Sense environments in October 2026, within a window of just over three minutes. The command ran under scheduler.exe and attempted to connect to 45.115.26[.]23 on port 4455. Cynet said the activity shares overlap with a November 2023 campaign in which actors likely linked to the CACTUS ransomware operation targeted Qlik Sense flaws, although the exact entry vulnerability in the latest activity is unknown.

In controlled testing, Cynet found the reverse shell could support reconnaissance and delivery of scripts intended to maintain access. One variant used a Windows Go reverse shell connecting to port 4456 and checked for Apache ActiveMQ processes; on Linux, it also attempted to gather system information and read the /etc/shadow and /etc/passwd files. Another variant tried to install OpenSSH and created a WinUpdCheck scheduled task that launched a PowerShell reverse shell every five minutes, while the actor’s exposed infrastructure contained an ActiveMQ exploit for CVE-2023-46604 and a modified Veeam toolchain for CVE-2024-40711.

  • CVE-2023-48365, known as DoubleQlik, was identified as an incomplete fix for the earlier Qlik Sense flaw CVE-2023-41265.
  • The observed operation used separate network ports for different purposes: port 4455 for the initial PowerShell reverse shell and port 4456 for a Windows Go-based backdoor.
  • The persistence mechanism used a scheduled task named WinUpdCheck to run a reverse-shell script every five minutes and attempted to enable remote access through OpenSSH.
  • The actor reused a legitimate OpenSSH package while adding an inbound firewall rule for TCP port 22, making the installation component itself less obviously malicious.

Attackers tried to break into Qlik Sense data-analysis servers used by several customers in the European Union, then open a hidden remote connection that would let them control the machines from afar. The attempts were blocked, but the attackers’ online toolkit also included ways to target Apache ActiveMQ and Veeam software, suggesting they may be preparing for broader break-ins. This matters because successful access could let criminals explore systems, keep returning through hidden access, and potentially take control of important business software.

The update covers flaws in Windows, Office, Developer Tools, SQL Server, and SharePoint Server, including 165 CVE identifiers not issued by Microsoft. Microsoft said a moderate-severity Outlook flaw, CVE-2026-124194, is being actively exploited. Microsoft released fixes for 1,259 security problems in its software, including a Microsoft Outlook issue that criminals are already using. Arctic Wolf Labs reported that Alibaba Cloud systems hosting the AntiFox AI penetration-testing platform were associated with malicious activity against internet-facing web services and Amazon Web Services (AWS) environments. AntiFox is an open-source, AI-driven platform designed to automate stages of an authorized penetration test, from reconnaissance through reporting. In observed intrusions, attackers used web exploitation and web shells to find configuration data, validate credentials, enumerate cloud services, access secrets, and conduct storage operations.

In one intrusion pattern, a compromised Microsoft IIS application was used to create an ASPX web shell through the IIS worker process, w3wp.exe. Commands then searched for web.config files and backups, read application settings and database connection strings, inspected logs, tested database access using extracted credentials, and copied files to a web-accessible upload directory. Arctic Wolf said the precise flaw used to execute code on the IIS server was unknown; in other cases, attackers began with valid AWS credentials obtained by undetermined means.

Using valid AWS identities, the activity enumerated many AWS services, including IAM, EC2, S3, Lambda, Secrets Manager, KMS, RDS, ECS, EKS, and Amazon Bedrock. Although many API requests were denied, researchers observed successful discovery activity, a GetSecretValue request for a production secret, and S3 discovery and object operations. The article places AntiFox within a broader rise of AI-powered agentic tools such as ARTEX, which can let operators assign an objective and automate reconnaissance, exploitation, and post-compromise steps at greater speed and scale.

  • A compromised web application can become a path into cloud environments because its configuration files may contain database connection strings and AWS credentials.
  • Even though many AWS service requests were denied, valid cloud identities still enabled successful discovery activity and, in some cases, access to a production secret and S3 object operations.
  • ARTEX operators reportedly often set an objective and then left agent fleets to work with little further interaction, showing that human involvement can be limited mainly to checking progress or changing priorities.
  • Internet exposure is itself a concern for these platforms: Censys identified 1,465 exposed ARTEX consoles, while Check Point found 10 ARTEX instances that exposed their full databases.
  • The article identifies roughly 45 open-source agentic attack frameworks that can connect language models to tools and act on their results autonomously.

Researchers found that attackers appear to have used AntiFox, an AI-powered testing tool, to break into public-facing websites and then reach Amazon Web Services accounts, including production secrets such as stored passwords or keys. The affected organizations are not named, but the activity involved their web servers, cloud accounts, databases, files, and internal services. This matters because AI tools can let attackers automate many steps of a break-in quickly and repeatedly, allowing even less-skilled criminals to search for weak systems and steal valuable access or data at a much larger scale.

eMudhra Revokes 8 More CAs It Previously Declared Unaffected by Key Compromise

eMudhra revoked eight additional intermediate certificate authorities after discovering their RSA private keys were exposed to a Python process during an HSM transfer procedure, despite previously saying they were unaffected. The incident expands the fallout from the company’s flawed key-ceremony script and accelerates the retirement of its publicly trusted TLS business.
KEY POINTS
  • 01eMudhra revoked eight additional intermediate certificate authorities after determining that their RSA private keys were read from hardware security modules into the memory of a Python process during an April 30, 2025 key ceremony.
  • 02The company had previously said the eight RSA certificate authorities were unaffected, but later concluded it could not demonstrate that handling of the key material complied with its own rules.
  • 03Six of the newly revoked certificate authorities issued website certificates and two issued code-signing certificates; eMudhra listed 195 certificates issued by them and says all holders have been moved to new certificates.
  • 04The same Python script reduced the private keys of eight separate ECDSA certificate authorities to a single leading byte, leading to their revocation in October.
  • 05eMudhra says it is exiting the publicly trusted TLS business, while Microsoft, Google Chrome, Firefox, and Apple are scheduled to withdraw trust from parts or all of its remaining certificate hierarchy on stated timelines.

eMudhra revoked eight additional intermediate certificate authorities after finding that their RSA private keys were read from hardware security modules into the memory of a Python process during an April 30, 2025 key ceremony. The company had previously described these CAs as unaffected, but later said it could not prove the key material was handled in accordance with its own rules. Six of the revoked CAs issued TLS website certificates and two issued code-signing certificates, with 195 certificates listed as having been issued from them.

The same in-house Python script had already caused an October compromise involving eight ECDSA CA keys by truncating each private value to its leading byte during a read-back operation. The weak ECDSA keys still generated valid signatures and passed linting and two WebTrust audit cycles, while invalid certificate-revocation-list signatures in June 2025 were an earlier sign of the problem. eMudhra says affected certificate holders have been moved to replacements and that it is exiting the publicly trusted TLS business, while Microsoft, Chrome, Firefox, and Apple are withdrawing trust from parts of its remaining certificate hierarchy on stated timelines.

  • The flawed process remained undetected through certificate linting and two WebTrust audit cycles because the weakened ECDSA keys could still create valid signatures.
  • Invalid certificate-revocation-list signatures in June 2025 were an early indicator of the underlying problem, but the company resolved them by signing with the weak keys that matched the issued certificates.
  • Certificate Transparency-enforcing browsers could not have been deceived by someone using the compromised October keys, but the article says it is unknown whether the keys were used against software that does not perform that check.
  • The newly revoked RSA authorities were revoked under “cessationOfOperation” rather than the “keyCompromise” reason used for the earlier affected authorities, prompting questions from participants in Mozilla’s bug thread.

eMudhra has canceled eight more certificate-issuing systems after finding that their secret signing keys were briefly copied into a computer program’s memory during setup, where the company cannot prove they stayed protected. These systems issued website and software-signing certificates for eMudhra, universities, colleges, a county, and other organizations, but the company says affected customers have received replacements. This matters because stolen certificate keys can let someone pretend to be a legitimate website or software publisher; the problem is also causing major browser and operating-system makers to remove trust in eMudhra certificates.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a significant certificate-authority incident involving additional revoked intermediate CAs, exposure of RSA private-key material during key handling, and the planned removal of eMudhra trust by major browser and operating-system vendors. Security professionals should assess affected certificates and anticipate trust-chain disruptions, although no misuse is known.

Over 35,000 Grok-Built Apps Exposed Online, Some Leaking Confidential Data and Passwords

Researchers found that more than 35,000 publicly accessible Grok-built apps could be discovered through passive DNS, with some exposing confidential corporate and personal data. Tests also showed Grok-generated authentication can be flawed, potentially allowing unauthorized users to access and alter app data.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Claroc found 37,571 Grok-built apps online, of which 35,578 were accessible without signing in.
  • 02About one in ten publicly accessible apps contained internal business or personal data, including employee lists, patient information, schedules, sales documents, and passwords stored in plain text.
  • 03The researchers found 24 publicly accessible apps created by staff at X and SpaceXSI, including a confidential sales-hire onboarding plan and an X advertising proposal marked confidential.
  • 04Grok Build selected "Anyone with the link" by default in the researchers' paid account, while app subdomains could be discovered through passive DNS records.
  • 05In a test app created by the researchers, Grok-generated sign-in code allowed an uninvited Google account to view, edit, and delete customer data.

Claroc researchers found 37,571 Grok-built apps online, including 35,578 that could be accessed without signing in. About one in ten of the open apps contained internal business or personal information, and roughly 2% were estimated to contain material serious enough to be rated high or critical. Exposed content included employee data, patient information, work schedules, confidential sales materials, and a timesheet application whose code contained employees’ passwords in plain text.

The researchers also identified 24 publicly accessible apps created by staff at X and SpaceXSI, although SpaceXSI later removed those staff apps. Grok Build’s publishing flow preselected “Anyone with the link” in the researchers’ paid account, while published app subdomains could be found through passive DNS records. In tests on their own apps, the researchers found that one Grok-generated sign-in implementation allowed an uninvited account to view, edit, and delete customer records because the code added a user to the team before checking authorization.

  • “Anyone with the link” was the preselected publishing option in the researchers’ paid Grok account, even though published app subdomains can be found through searchable DNS lookup records.
  • In the researchers’ test, Grok-generated access control added a person to a sales team before checking whether they were authorized, allowing an uninvited account to read, edit, and delete records.
  • Setting a Grok app to “Only you” returned a 401 error to an outsider for both the app page and its data, while unpublishing removed an app from the internet within seconds.
  • Although SpaceXSI said employee accounts default to “Only you,” Claroc found 24 apps made by SpaceXSI and X staff that were open to anyone.

Researchers found more than 35,000 apps made with Grok that could be opened by anyone online, including some containing private company and personal information. Exposed material included employee lists, a patient briefing, work schedules, sales documents, and passwords stored in readable form. The problem affects organizations whose staff used Grok to create and publish apps, because app web addresses can be found even when their names are difficult to guess. Tests also showed that one Grok-made sign-in system let an unapproved person view, change, and delete customer records.

We Built An Agent That Broke All of Our Security Rules. Here's What We Learned.

Browser-based AI agents often operate inside a user’s authenticated session, making their actions indistinguishable from the user’s and potentially granting excessive, untraceable access. Organizations should inventory and constrain these agents, require step-up approval for sensitive actions, and push for standards that convey agent identity, human delegation, and task-scoped permissions.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Token’s Rehearsal browser agent operates within a user’s authenticated session, so the application server cannot inherently distinguish its clicks from the user’s clicks.
  • 02Token configured Rehearsal to lock and dim the application while it acts, record every action including blocked ones, and use read-only dashboard access unless the user approves a change.
  • 03The article says current approaches such as browser controls, WebMCP, and Web Bot Auth provide partial information but do not combine agent identity, the person it represents, and a narrower task-specific permission scope.
  • 04The article recommends that organizations inventory browser and endpoint agents, map them to users and owners, review their access, and require explicit approval or stronger sign-in checks for sensitive or irreversible actions.

Token built a browser agent called Rehearsal that answers questions in its platform by navigating pages, setting filters, and filling in forms. Because it operates inside a user’s authenticated browser session, the application server cannot inherently distinguish the agent’s clicks from the user’s. This breaks the usual goals of separate agent identity, limited permissions, and activity records that are distinct from a human’s.

Because Token controls both Rehearsal and its application, it can identify when the agent is driving, lock and dim the interface, record its actions, and restrict it to read-only dashboards unless a user approves a change. The article says browser controls, WebMCP, and Web Bot Auth each address parts of the problem but do not jointly provide agent identity, proof of the person delegating the task, and a narrower task-specific permission scope. Until standards can carry those signals together, organizations should discover agents that use human sessions, review their access, audit their activity, and require explicit approval or stronger sign-in checks for sensitive or irreversible actions.

  • A browser agent can be useful precisely because it works inside a person’s signed-in session, but that same design means it automatically inherits the person’s full reach unless additional limits are imposed.
  • Token’s experience shows that an application can reduce agent risk by giving the agent less access than the signed-in user, such as read-only access and requiring user approval before saving changes.
  • Existing efforts address separate parts of the problem: browsers may know an agent is controlling a session, WebMCP can label actions by consequence, and Web Bot Auth can identify an agent, but none alone establishes who delegated the task and what the agent is permitted to do.
  • Organizations can reduce risk before standards mature by treating actions from human-session-based agents as delegated access, discovering them, constraining them, auditing them, and adding passkey prompts for high-impact actions.

Token built a browser helper called Rehearsal that can navigate its website and fill in forms for a user, then found that it naturally acts with the same access as the person who is signed in. This means many similar helpers could read or change things that their user can access, while websites may have no way to tell whether a person or a helper made the action. Companies, browser makers, and software providers need ways to show who a helper is working for, limit it to only the task it was given, and keep a clear record of what it did. Until those protections are common, organizations should find these helpers, restrict what they can do, and ask people to confirm important or permanent actions.

Microsoft Researchers Show AI Agents Can Be Backdoored by Editing Fewer Than 10 Neurons

Microsoft researchers showed that an attacker with access to an AI model’s weights can implant a hidden agent backdoor by directly modifying fewer than 10 dormant neurons, causing trigger-based execution of attacker commands while largely preserving normal model behavior. The finding underscores the need to verify model provenance and checkpoint integrity, sandbox agent actions, and restrict permissions.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Microsoft researchers demonstrated Lazarus, a method for adding a hidden backdoor to an AI model by directly editing fewer than 10 rarely used neurons without retraining the full model.
  • 02When a selected trigger appears in a user request or tool output, the edited model can generate an attacker-chosen command that an AI agent may execute with its own permissions.
  • 03In tests on Nemotron-Terminal-8B, seven edited neurons produced a harmless marker command in at least 98.8% of triggered recorded sessions and in none of the checked trigger-free sessions.
  • 04The researchers said that anyone able to modify a model checkpoint before deployment, including insiders, compromised build-pipeline users, or publishers of altered public models, could plant this type of backdoor.
  • 05Microsoft recommends verifying checkpoints against their declared base models, obtaining models from original publishers, restricting agent permissions, isolating agent-generated code, limiting outbound connections, and requiring human approval for high-impact actions.

Microsoft researchers demonstrated a method called Lazarus that can implant a hidden backdoor in an AI model by directly editing fewer than 10 rarely used neurons, without retraining the model. When a chosen trigger appears in a user request or a tool’s output, the modified model can generate an attacker-selected command for an AI agent to run with its existing permissions. The researchers tested the technique on Nemotron-Terminal-8B, Qwen3.6-27B, and Gemma-4-31B-IT, and said they had not observed threat actors using it.

On Nemotron-Terminal-8B, the team altered and tuned seven neurons in the final feed-forward layer using 23 example sessions, causing a harmless test command to appear in at least 98.8% of triggered recorded sessions and none of the checked trigger-free sessions. The altered models could still perform normally on ordinary evaluations, although one Qwen version’s Terminal-Bench result declined from 46.59% to 42.05%. Microsoft said the principal risk is to organizations using AI agents with powerful access, because anyone able to modify a model checkpoint before deployment could plant the backdoor; recommended defenses include checking models against their original weights, restricting agent permissions, isolating generated code, limiting outbound network access, and requiring approval for high-impact actions.

  • The potential harm is driven more by the permissions granted to an AI agent than by the small size of the model edit, because a generated command can download and run any remote script the agent is allowed to execute.
  • The backdoor can be triggered by text returned from a tool, not only by a user’s request, creating a path in which apparently routine agent interactions activate the hidden behavior.
  • Ordinary model-quality tests may not expose the alteration: the edited Qwen models retained most math-test performance and had a relatively limited drop on the Terminal-Bench agent-task test.
  • Comparing a deployed checkpoint with its known original version is the most reliable proposed detection approach, while a detector tested without an original copy missed some edits and falsely flagged some clean models.
  • The researchers found that asking AI models themselves to inspect checkpoints was unreliable, with Claude Opus 5.5 classifying 41% of edited checkpoints as clean.

Microsoft researchers found that someone who can alter an AI model’s saved settings can secretly change fewer than 10 rarely used parts of it so it follows an attacker’s command when it sees a chosen phrase or message. This could affect people and organizations that use AI assistants able to run commands, because the assistant may download or run harmful software using whatever access it has been given. The altered model can still appear to work normally, so checking where AI models came from, limiting what they are allowed to do, and requiring human approval for important actions are important safeguards.

DKIM Passed for the Wrong Company: An HMRC Lure

An HMRC-themed phishing email passed DKIM only because it was sent through an authenticated third-party account, while SPF and DMARC failed for the visible sender domain. The case shows that a DKIM pass does not validate the claimed sender and that DMARC p=none provides monitoring rather than protection.
KEY POINTS
  • 01A UK communications company received an HMRC-themed email titled "Update your contact information" that used the display name "Government Gateway."
  • 02The email’s DKIM signature passed for the domain of an authenticated third-party mail account, not for the Japanese company domain shown in the From address.
  • 03Google recorded SPF as a soft fail and DMARC as a failure for the visible sender domain, whose DMARC policy was set to p=none.
  • 04The message’s Update button directed recipients to a path on an Argentine construction company’s website, while the GOV.UK logo linked to the real GOV.UK site.
  • 05IRONSCALES marked the button destination as malicious and closed the incident in a final Malicious Content state through Adaptive AI analysis.

A UK communications company received an HMRC-style email titled “Update your contact information,” using the display name “Government Gateway.” The visible From address and Return-Path belonged to a Japanese company domain, while the message’s Update button led to a path on an Argentine construction company website. The email threatened that the recipient’s Government Gateway user ID and profile would be deleted unless its business VAT information was updated.

The message passed DKIM for a different domain: the domain of an account used to submit the message through an authenticated Japanese mail relay. Google recorded SPF as a soft fail and DMARC as a failure for the visible sender domain, but the DMARC policy was p=none, which reports failures without requiring action. IRONSCALES scored the button destination as malicious, identified an exact display-name impersonation of Government Gateway, and closed the incident as Malicious Content through Adaptive AI analysis.

  • A passing DKIM result can be technically valid while offering no assurance that the visible sender or brand being impersonated is legitimate, because it may only confirm that an unrelated authenticated account sent the message.
  • A DMARC policy of p=none records authentication failures but does not instruct receiving systems to block or quarantine the message, leaving a delivery path for unaligned mail.
  • The email used real HMRC-hosted images and linked its GOV.UK logo to the legitimate site, while placing the malicious destination only behind the action button, making superficial link checking less useful.
  • The absence of a Message-ID from the submitting client, followed by Google adding one on arrival, was consistent with direct scripted SMTP submission according to the article.

A UK communications company received a fake-looking HMRC message that urged someone to update their details or risk having their Government Gateway profile deleted. Although one technical check showed the email had been sent through a real account, that account did not match the sender shown to the reader, and the update button led to an unrelated Argentine construction website. This matters because criminals can combine trusted-looking government branding, real email services, and alarming deadlines to trick people into clicking harmful links, while weak email protections may only record the warning instead of stopping the message.

A researcher using the GitHub account Oracle-Security publicly disclosed Able2Shell on November 9, describing 33 alleged vulnerabilities in N-able N-central and providing proof-of-concept code. The findings include four reported exploit chains, with one XXE-based chain described as requiring no credentials and allowing commands to run as the nable account. Two reported chains can reach root-level command execution. N-able characterized the disclosure as involving critical vulnerabilities.

On November 10, N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2, build 2026.4.1.26, to address seven CVEs with CVSSv4 scores from 8.3 to 9.3. The patched issues include XML external entity flaws, server-side request forgery, OGNL injection, path traversal leading to remote code execution, local privilege escalation, and stored cross-site scripting. N-able has not mapped the seven CVEs to all 33 findings, and it said a further hotfix would provide additional security updates. Hosted N-central servers were upgraded globally, while on-premises customers must update their own servers and are advised to keep them offline until they do.

N-able reported scanning activity associated with the published proof-of-concept code, and Beazley Security Labs and Previdian reported exploitation attempts against honeypot and decoy N-central systems. As of November 10, no confirmed compromise of a customer server had been reported. Organizations are advised to review login and authentication activity from November 8 onward and watch for unusual remote-access sessions, newly deployed scripts, and unauthorized administrator accounts.

  • The seven published CVEs are not a complete accounting of the 33 reported findings, because N-able has not said which findings each CVE covers and has planned an additional hotfix.
  • The reported MMS3 attack chains require an administrator to view poisoned patch details before the planted code runs, unlike the reported XXE chain, which the researcher describes as requiring no credentials.
  • On-premises customers are advised to keep N-central servers offline until they can apply the update, while hosted N-central servers were upgraded by N-able.
  • Customers must upgrade Agents before Probes because an upgraded Probe cannot communicate with Agents that have not yet been upgraded.
  • Hotfix 2 removes legacy mobile device management and temporarily disables N-central's built-in remote-control feature, although Take Control remains available.

A researcher publicly shared 33 claimed security flaws in N-able’s N-central, software organizations use to manage computers and networks, including one claimed route that could let an outsider run commands without logging in. N-able issued an update that fixes seven of the most serious problems and upgraded its hosted service, while customers running their own servers need to apply the update. Attempts to use the published instructions have been seen against decoy systems, but no confirmed customer break-in had been reported as of November 10. The stakes are high because successful use could give attackers control of the management system and, in some cases, the underlying server.

Citrus Ransomware: VLESS for traffic, Sn00py for encryption, and LLMs lending a hand

Citrus Ransomware targets Russian organizations by abusing compromised contractor accounts, escalating privileges, and spreading Sn00py ransomware through malicious Group Policy Objects. The group combines familiar tools with VLESS/Xray tunnels and apparent LLM-generated scripts, making tight control of third-party access and early detection critical.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Citrus Ransomware gained initial access through contractor employee credentials stolen to connect to corporate VPNs or internet-facing RDP terminal servers.
  • 02The group attempted to escalate privileges by exploiting CVE-2026-54121 (Certighost), which could allow it to authenticate as a domain controller after obtaining a forged certificate.
  • 03Citrus used Xray reverse VLESS tunnels over port 443 with REALITY settings designed to disguise its traffic as requests to legitimate Yandex sites.
  • 04Before encryption, the attackers collected Telegram Desktop session-related data, archived it with 7-Zip, and uploaded it to an external web service through Google Chrome.
  • 05Citrus deployed Go-based Sn00py ransomware through malicious Group Policy Objects, encrypting user files with a .citrus extension and disabling Windows Defender and Volume Shadow Copy as part of the deployment.

Citrus Ransomware is a previously undocumented group that targeted Russian companies by using stolen contractor credentials to access corporate VPNs or internet-facing Remote Desktop servers. The group then tried to gain higher privileges, move between systems, collect credentials and messaging-app data, and disable security protections. Its activity combines widely available tools with VLESS tunnels intended to make its communications resemble ordinary HTTPS traffic and apparent LLM-generated commands and scripts.

Citrus attempted to exploit CVE-2026-54121 (Certighost) to obtain certificates that could let it authenticate as a domain controller, and it also targeted insecurely configured 1C:Enterprise servers. It used Xray reverse VLESS tunnels over port 443, AnyDesk for remote control, and tools including mimikatz, Snaffler, ADRecon, SharpHound, and fscan. Before encryption, it archived data associated with Telegram Desktop sessions and uploaded it to an external web service.

For impact, the group deployed Go-based Sn00py ransomware through malicious Group Policy Objects, encrypting user files with the .citrus extension and leaving CITRUS_README.txt ransom notes. The malicious policy disabled Windows Defender and the Volume Shadow Copy service, enabled WinRM, created a scheduled task to launch the ransomware, and excluded selected domain controllers from encryption so distribution could continue. The incidents highlight the importance of tightly controlling and restricting contractor access, which Citrus used for initial entry.

  • Comments embedded in otherwise routine commands and PowerShell scripts were unusual for the attackers and were assessed as likely evidence of LLM-generated or LLM-edited content.
  • The ransomware configuration excluded specific domain controllers from encryption, allowing the malicious Group Policy used to distribute the ransomware to continue propagating across the network.
  • Citrus did not only disable security software on individual hosts; after gaining sufficient privileges, it also targeted centralized security-management consoles to disable protection at scale.
  • Xray configuration files were sometimes deleted immediately after the tunnel started, reducing the evidence available to defenders while retaining remote access.
  • Citrus and Toy Ghouls were observed compromising the same infrastructure in several incidents, while sharing Russian-language targeting, tools, directories, and several operating methods.

The article describes Citrus, a newly documented criminal group that breaks into Russian companies by using stolen accounts belonging to contractors who can access company systems. The group steals passwords and messaging-app data, turns off security protections, and locks files for ransom using software called Sn00py. It also hides its communications to make them look like ordinary website traffic and appears to use AI tools to help create some commands and scripts. The cases show that a weakly protected outside contractor can become a path to disruption, data theft, and company-wide file encryption.

A Constella Intelligence infostealer log from a potential Binance employee’s MacBook Air shows the browser reached macdev.slab.com through a Google ad on 24 March 2026. A same-day Homebrew GitHub report identified that domain as a sponsored fake Homebrew installer page offering a malicious command. Sixteen seconds after the ad click, an osascript process was running, and the report found artifacts consistent with the MacSync stealer. The log does not contain the exact page URL, command, or browser history.

The stolen data included the Mac login password, Chrome Keychain data, 532 saved credentials across 365 services, and credentials for Binance-related data-platform tools including Kibana, Airflow, Kafka, Zeppelin, and Git. The report says the exposed Okta password was a variant of the Mac login password and that passwords for 15 other corporate email accounts were also present. Some browser sessions were still nominally valid as of 4 November 2026. Although the incident predates Binance’s reported $6.34 billion theft, the article states there is no evidence that this log was used in that attack and notes that the date and systems in the log do not match Binance’s disclosed Wallet DevOps compromise.

  • The browser cookie timestamps and recorded Asia/Taipei time zone allowed the report to align the Mac’s local process times with the Google ad click and rule out a larger UTC offset.

Unit 42 identified Falcon, also known as XG or Xiàng Gē, a command-and-control framework that compromises browser sessions through malicious JavaScript placed on websites. Between March and May 2026, observed campaigns targeted government entities in one Middle Eastern country and four Southeast Asian countries, including foreign affairs, defense, interior, law enforcement and justice organizations. Falcon was used to steal passwords, emails, session cookies and communications, and it also served as a delivery mechanism for the Rust-based Antino implant.

Falcon can maintain a persistent encrypted WebSocket connection from a compromised browser tab and execute arbitrary JavaScript supplied by an operator. Its Chrome and Firefox extensions masquerade as a PDF viewer, request 40 permissions, and can collect credentials, cookies, browsing history, downloads, clipboard contents, network traffic, and selected messaging data. The extension can also use a victim’s browser as a proxy with the victim’s saved login state, intercept and replace downloads, and capture internal documents. Antino establishes Windows Registry persistence and uses Microsoft OneDrive to exchange heartbeat data, commands and files with its operators.

  • Falcon’s management panel hides its login screen until F9 is pressed three times and otherwise presents a blank page, while its public-facing server can display Tetris or Snake to avoid drawing attention.
  • Falcon stores its victim identifier in local storage and cookies using Baidu Analytics-like Hm_lvt_ names, which can make attacker tracking data appear similar to ordinary web analytics artifacts.
  • The malicious browser extension can turn an affected browser into a proxy that uses the victim’s saved login state, allowing the operator to request internal resources as the victim.
  • Falcon can intercept a legitimate download, cancel it, remove its download-history entry, and substitute an operator-controlled file while keeping the original filename.
  • Antino uses Microsoft OneDrive for its communications, writing heartbeat files and receiving commands through files in OneDrive folders rather than using a conventional dedicated control server.

Researchers found a tool called Falcon that lets attackers take control of what happens inside a person’s web browser after secretly adding harmful code to websites or installing a fake browser add-on disguised as a PDF viewer. It was used against government organizations in one Middle Eastern country and four Southeast Asian countries, including foreign affairs, defense, police, and justice bodies. The attackers could steal passwords, emails, private messages, login information, and internal documents, and could even use a victim’s logged-in browser to reach restricted resources. This matters because browser-based spying can hide within normal web use and give attackers long-term access to highly sensitive government information.

Unit 42 reports that attackers are using AI-enabled red-teaming and penetration-testing tools, including ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI, to autonomously conduct offensive operations. The organization observed ARTEX in intrusion attempts against multiple targets, including cases where attacker infrastructure hosted an ARTEX console or used ARTEX-associated infrastructure and user agents. ARTEX is described as an open-source, multi-agent AI penetration-testing framework that can evaluate responses, adapt after failures, and continue pursuing an objective. Unit 42 states that attackers can use it against internet-exposed identity workflows and APIs, then use obtained credentials and trust relationships to reach cloud environments.

As of October 2026, Unit 42 identified 1,323 internet-facing CyberStrikeAI hosts and 609 ARTEX hosts, with 21 running both tools. Observed behavior associated with autonomous tooling included request bursts followed by 25–31 second pauses, rapid credential validation, immediate targeting of paths disclosed in OpenAPI specifications and source maps, retries after HTTP 422 errors, and repeated polling loops. Unit 42 recommends reducing public exposure by removing public attack maps and exposed tokens, authenticating every write endpoint, strengthening password-reset and registration flows, moving secrets into a secrets manager, and enforcing least privilege. It also advises detecting behavior such as canary usernames, cloud-key use from new IP addresses, write-then-delete storage tests, and early probing that precedes later intrusion activity.

These tools can quickly try password-reset pages, application connections, and exposed digital keys, then change their approach when something fails. Organizations of any size or industry with publicly reachable systems may be affected, because this automation lets attackers test many targets at once. Log Analysis Field Guide: Tips for Spotting Patterns and Red Flags

This guide explains how to analyze logs by focusing on timestamps, repetition, normal behavior baselines, and targeted filtering to identify suspicious activity. Key red flags include repeated failed logins followed by success, after-hours access, impossible travel, unexpected account changes, and unusual processes or network connections.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Logs record digital activity such as logins, file downloads, and network connections, helping answer who performed an action, what happened, when it happened, and where it originated.
  • 02Core log elements commonly include a timestamp, source system, event type, user or process, and whether the activity succeeded or failed.
  • 03Analysts should look for repetition, suspicious timing, and behavior that differs from normal activity, while using filters to focus on relevant entries.
  • 04Red flags include repeated failed logins followed by a successful login, unexpected after-hours activity, impossible travel indicators, modified accounts, and unusual processes or connections.
  • 05The article recommends documenting searches, checking whether activity has occurred before, comparing it with known bad behavior, and deciding whether escalation is needed.

Log analysis involves reviewing automatically generated records of logins, file downloads, network connections, and other system activity to determine who did what, when, and where. Common log fields include timestamps, source systems, event types, users or processes, and success or failure outcomes. The article emphasizes that analysts do not need to understand every entry, but should learn to identify meaningful patterns.

Analysts should establish what normal activity looks like, use filters to focus on relevant events, and document their searches. Important warning signs include repeated failed logins followed by success, unexpected after-hours access, impossible-travel indicators, account or permission changes, and unusual processes or outbound connections. Impossible-travel findings should be verified against source logs because VPN endpoints, cloud proxies, and mobile-device synchronization can produce false positives.

  • A single failed login may be a typing mistake, but ten failed attempts within two minutes are a pattern worth investigating.
  • An impossible-travel alert can indicate compromised credentials, but VPN endpoints, cloud proxies, and mobile device synchronization can also create false positives, so the source logs should be verified.
  • Failed events can be more informative than successful ones because a sequence of failed attempts followed by success may show that someone guessed a password.
  • Establishing normal behavior, such as typical transfer volumes or scheduled maintenance access, makes unusual activity easier to identify and reduces unnecessary escalation.
  • Documenting searches lets an analyst retrace the investigation rather than relying on memory.

This article is a beginner’s guide to reading the automatic records that computers and applications create when people sign in, download files, or make connections. It explains how to notice warning signs such as many failed password attempts, unusual late-night activity, or a person appearing to log in from far-apart places within minutes. This matters to anyone whose workplace or personal accounts use computers, because these records can help find unauthorized access or data being sent to unknown places before the problem becomes much larger.

MAY · 60 research 11 Nov 2026 02:00 UTC · gpt-5.6-terra

Every PC has a junk drawer, and attackers know it

Acronis telemetry from 1.8 million business computers finds that forgotten and unsupported software, plus overdue third-party patches, remain widespread—often affecting commonly exploited apps such as WinRAR, Java, Firefox, and 7-Zip. Organizations should inventory software, remove end-of-support products, enable and monitor third-party patching, and prioritize older Windows systems and small-business environments.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Acronis analyzed anonymized telemetry from more than 1.8 million business computers that were online on September 30, 2026, finding that the average Windows PC had 38 installed applications.
  • 02Among Windows PCs with available update data, 22.1% had at least one security update for an everyday application that had remained uninstalled for more than 30 days, and 77% of those waiting updates addressed a known-exploited weakness.
  • 03Nearly one quarter of Windows PCs (22.8%) ran at least one product that was past end of support, including older Microsoft Office versions, Silverlight, Adobe Flash Player, and legacy Java releases.
  • 04Security updates for Chrome and Firefox were installed in median times of four and six days, respectively, while WinRAR updates took 35 days and Java updates installed in the quarter had a median age of 1,000 days.
  • 05Windows 10 and older systems had substantially more end-of-support software than Windows 11 systems, with 49.6% of Windows 10 PCs and 80.4% of Windows 7 and 8.x PCs affected, compared with 17.0% of Windows 11 PCs.

Acronis analyzed anonymized telemetry from more than 1.8 million business computers online on September 30, 2026, finding that the average Windows PC carried 38 applications and 22.3% had more than 50. Of Windows applications with a known install date, 25.6% had been installed for more than three years. Nearly one Windows PC in four, 22.8%, ran at least one product whose maker no longer supports it, including older Microsoft Office versions, Silverlight, Adobe Flash Player, and legacy Java versions.

Among Windows PCs with update data, 22.1% had at least one third-party application security update waiting for more than 30 days, and 77% of those waiting updates fixed weaknesses known to be exploited by criminals. WinRAR, Java, Firefox, Notepad++, and 7-Zip were the applications most often associated with overdue updates, while browsers updated much faster than tools such as WinRAR, VLC, UltraVNC, and Java. The report recommends removing unsupported software, expanding update scanning and third-party patching to every managed PC, reviewing stalled approvals, schedules, and restarts, and prioritizing older Windows systems and the smallest customer environments.

  • Turning on third-party patching reduces overdue updates compared with scanning alone, but it does not eliminate the problem: 22.4% of PCs with patching enabled still had an update waiting for more than 30 days, versus 31.3% of scan-only PCs.
  • The report found that most overdue app updates were not merely theoretical risks: on 77% of affected PCs, the waiting update fixed a weakness already known to be used by criminals.
  • Update visibility is itself a major gap, because update data was available for only 41.5% of the Windows PCs studied, while PCs without update data ran end-of-support products at about the same rate as PCs with data.
  • Small customers with 1 to 10 computers had the lowest update-data coverage and the highest rates of end-of-support software and apps unchanged for two years or more.
  • Browsers that update themselves were patched within days, while tools that may require manual action, including WinRAR, remote-control software, VLC, and Java, often remained behind for weeks, months, or years.

Acronis reviewed data from more than 1.8 million business computers and found that many still contain old, unused, or no-longer-supported programs. More than one in five Windows computers had a security update waiting for over a month, often for everyday tools such as WinRAR, Java, Firefox, and 7-Zip, and nearly one in four had software whose maker no longer provides fixes. This matters because criminals can use known weaknesses in neglected programs to get into business computers, especially at smaller companies and on older versions of Windows.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a substantive telemetry-based report on software inventory, unsupported products, and overdue third-party updates across more than 1.8 million business computers. It offers useful benchmarks and prioritization data, but it does not report a specific active incident, newly disclosed flaw, or urgent patch.

ENISA Threat Landscape 2026 research
ENISA
The article cites this threat landscape for its finding that vulnerabilities were used in six in ten unauthorized-access incidents where the entry method was known.
2026 Data Breach Investigations Report research
Verizon
The article references the report's finding that vulnerability use was the most common known entry route in breaches and that only 26% of known-exploited critical weaknesses were fully fixed.
Cyber Security Breaches Survey 2025/26 research
UK Government
The article cites the survey to show that only 34% of businesses reported having a rule to install security updates within 14 days.
NIST Guide to Patch Management guide
National Institute of Standards and Technology
The article references the guide's recommendation that effective patch management begins with a complete inventory of software on every computer.
Gartner survey of senior risk managers research
Gartner
The article cites the survey's identification of AI-assisted discovery of weaknesses as the top emerging risk.
